newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Quinnsworth workers, suppliers await news on Tesco.
newsitem.headline: Quinnsworth workers, suppliers await news on Tesco.

text.p: Irish supermarket workers and suppliers waited anxiously on Thursday for news on talks between British supermarket group Tesco Plc and Associated British Foods (ABF).

Tesco was reported to be close to clinching a 600 million pound ($961.5 million) deal for ABF's Quinnsworth Group in the Republic of Ireland and its Northern Ireland grocery operations, Stewarts and Crazy Prices.

The deal, which would be the largest ever in the Irish grocery trade, would give Tesco a 26 percent share of the market in the Republic and a 30 percent share in Northern Ireland, Irish newspapers said.
A Tesco spokeswoman confirmed the two boards were in talks but gave no further comment while Quinnsworth declined to comment.
But analysts said that if the deal went ahead, it would represent a major shake-up of the Irish grocery trade with major implications for shoppers, suppliers and those working in the industry.
The Mandate trade union, which represents 7,000 Quinnsworth employees in 67 outlets, said its members ought to be told what was happening.

"We have written to Quinnsworth and asked them to confirm or deny the very strong rumour which was circulating yesterday that the company has been taken over by Tesco," John Douglas, assistant general manager of Mandate, told Irish state radio.
"Up to this morning, they have failed to do so. It is an unsatisfactory situation to put their 7,000 employees in. They deserve to know."
But Douglas said Mandate would have no problems dealing with Tesco which entered the Irish market in the 1980s but withdrew in 1986 with accumulated losses of around 20 million.
"We have dealt with Tesco in the past as a trade union...We had a very reasonable relationship with Tesco.

"As a retailer they are very well spoken of and they trade very successfully in the UK. But we would certainly want assurances vis-a-vis the number of jobs, job entitlements and also the terms and conditions of employment," Douglas said.

Irish suppliers are also nervous about the implications of such a takeover, fearing that a supermarket giant like Tesco could impose tougher demands on suppliers in terms of price and deliveries or replace Irish suppliers with British ones.

"It's not the name over the door that worries us but because the UK multiple has such massive buying power and distribution already in place," Ciaran Fitzgerald, director of food and drink at the Irish Business and Employers Confederation said.
But analysts say the consumer should benefit from the increased competition provided by British retailers who have entered the Irish market in droves of late.

Boots, Debenhams and Dixons are among the big British names to have arrived in Ireland in the last year, drawn by the fastest-growing economy in the European Union and a large young population, analysts say.
The British supermarket chains have already established a toehold in Northern Ireland where Tesco opened a Belfast store last year.
But they have run into planning difficulties there, making the takeover of existing operations a more attractive option.

Aside from the ABF/Tesco talks, British supermarket chain Safeway Plc is reported to be in talks with Fitzwilton about the purchase of a major stake in its Wellworth chain of supermarkets in Northern Ireland.
